evidence: The books on São Paulo photographic albums and Museu Paulista collections connect directly to the articles on Militão photographs and the museum's photographic collections. USP confirms the ORCID holder is its Museu Paulista photography and visual-culture curator.

The CAPES key supplies no works, dates or institution. USP confirms the book author's museum career, but no evidence connects capes-person:525091 to that career; the matching name alone is insufficient.

Uppsala identifies Skrå, stad och stat (1991) as Lindström's dissertation and describes his subsequent research on urban households and Nordic homicide, directly connecting both article subjects to the book author's career.

UBC Press identifies the author of What Is Water? as a geography professor at Queen's University, matching the H-Water review credit's institution and its contemporaneous work on rivers and human relationships with water.
The University of Zurich bibliography for James T.C. Liu (1919–1993) lists both the Pittsburgh 1950 dissertation Sino-Japanese diplomacy during the appeasement period and Reform in Sung China (1959).

The 1978 dissertation studies the precolonial economic history of the Avongara-Azande in Africa. The other key's established career concerns English buildings, railway architecture and historic towns, with books already appearing in 1967–1968; the works do not connect.

Playing the Man (1998), catalogued under Anne Spencer Lombard, studies male socialization and masculinity in New England, 1675–1765. Making Manhood (2003) continues precisely that research on growing up male in colonial New England.

Long's own CV lists the November 2015 H-Net Cantwell review alongside The New Left, Where the Sun Never Shines, The Writer's Portable Mentor and Crossing Over, directly linking the reviewer to the books.

José Sérgio Leite Lopes's books trace Brazilian sugar workers, industrial class conflict and pollution politics. José Mota da Lopes is a differently named reviewer of southern African regional cooperation, credited to Binghamton/Syracuse; no works connect the two careers.

The books on nineteenth-century Brazilian and Argentine natural-history museums connect directly to the articles on those museums' formation, paleontology and international exchanges, forming a continuous specialized research programme from 1990 onward.
The GND record 11244850X explicitly links to LC authority n82011303, VIAF 94637417 and ISNI 0000000110313789, establishing that both keys identify the same Nicole Loraux.

The public ORCID record contains only the name Christopher Loss, with no works, biography, affiliations or external links. It therefore provides no independent connection to the author of Between Citizens and the State.

The 2009 UFMG thesis on Ouro Preto population and families continues the 2008 book's study of marriage and families in Vila Rica/Ouro Preto into the later nineteenth century. The thesis itself cites Lott's Na forma do ritual romano (2008).

Maria Rita Garcia Loureiro's books concern rural capitalism, economists, bureaucracy and democratic government. Maria Rosalina Bulcão Loureiro's article studies Indigenous and mixed-race women accused of prostitution in eighteenth-century Maranhão; both the full names and research careers differ.

The Canadian Civil War dissertation dates to 1926, eighty years before Human Remains (2006). The publisher identifies the latter author as a contemporary Melbourne historian of dissection and anatomy; the chronology and subjects describe separate careers.
